body:
## Outcome wanted

After the closed-form dual finds the objective bound, reliably recover a **feasible continuous path** (the step-1 primal) that lands **near the bound**, and have that recovery **respect inertia** so it matches MC instead of diverging from it. This is an outcome, not a method: any approach that meets the acceptance criteria below qualifies. A leading candidate (branch and bound) and alternatives are listed, but picking the method is itself part of the work (see Deliverables).

## Background: why the recovery is the weak step

The solve has three logically separate jobs:

1. Compute the objective ceiling (the weak-duality bound). `ClosedFormSolve.dualBound` / `CostateDualSolver`. This works.
2. **Recover a feasible continuous path** near the bound. `ClosedFormSolve.recover` reads the dual costates into per-tick yaws. This is the weak step, and the subject of this issue.
3. Snap that path onto the byte-exact sine lattice and land it.

The bound (1) is only a number. The recovery (2) turns it into a playable path. On coupled multi-jump problems the recovery is degenerate (the LCvx unique-inner-maximizer condition fails), so it returns a path that violates constraints in **pure continuous space**, before any Minecraft or quantization. There is then nothing feasible for the lattice snap to work on. So closed form fails at the recovery, not at the lattice.

Two findings from the loopmm 3-jump fixture (`core/src/test/resources/captures/loopmm-3jump-lands.json`, 1.8.9, MAX Z@71), a jump provably feasible (a hand path lands it at Z = -279.29973):

**A. The recovery is infeasible in continuous space.** The dual bound is -279.299033 (a valid ceiling). The recovered continuous path "reaches" Z = -279.045898 only by violating the tick-61 wall by **0.245 blocks**, measured in the linear model with no sine table and no inertia. The bound is a correct ceiling; the recovery cannot produce a feasible path that attains it (best feasible continuous is approximately -279.29906, a small duality gap).

**B. Inertia, not the sine table, is the dominant continuous-to-MC mismatch.** Same recovered yaws across three models (linear / sine-only / full byte-exact):

| | linear (cont) | sine-only | full | sine part | inertia part |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Z @ tick61 | -282.580189 | -282.580206 | -282.548942 | -0.000017 | **+0.031264** |
| Z @ final | -279.045898 | -279.045832 | -279.012925 | +0.000066 | **+0.032907** |
| X @ final | -27.547146 | -27.546511 | -27.570146 | +0.000635 | **-0.023635** |

Max over all ticks: inertia Z 3.3e-2 / X 2.4e-2; sine Z 8.3e-5 / X 6.3e-4. At the binding Z@61 wall inertia is ~1800x the sine term. Mechanism: `vz = -0.0037` at tick 41 falls under the 0.005 per-axis threshold and is zeroed, propagating to 0.031 of Z error by tick 61, which flips the path from continuous-feasible to byte-infeasible. So the recovery model omits the single biggest error term. Inertia is **piecewise-affine**, so unlike the discrete sine table it can be folded into the recovery.

## Acceptance criteria (method-agnostic)

- On a problem where `ClosedFormSolve.optimize` currently returns null from degenerate recovery (loopmm), the recovery returns a continuous-feasible path that is **at or near the bound** (the right basin), not merely feasible in the greedy basin.
- The recovery reproduces MC's per-axis inertia zeroing: a recovered path evaluated continuously vs byte-exact differs by the **sine residual only** (order 1e-4 or less), not by the inertia term (order 1e-2). Verify on loopmm that the inertia contribution drops out.
- Any new constraints (inertia, basin pins) are valid linear constraints reusing `JumpLinearModel.Wall` / `compileWalls`, not a new bespoke model.
- `dualBound` is unchanged where no inertia tick is active; no regression on the `:core:test` capture suite.
- A capture-driven check covers the reachable-but-currently-missed case.

## Sub-task 1: fold inertia into the recovery (low-risk, mostly settled)

Per-axis momentum cancellation (0.005 in 1.8.x, 0.003 in 1.12.x, combined-XZ 9.0E-6 for modern players) is **piecewise-affine**, so it folds into the recovery model directly. Per near-threshold tick/axis there are three affine cases: `v >= +thr`, `v <= -thr`, or `|v| < thr` forcing `v = 0`. Velocity is affine in the inputs, so each is a linear velocity wall in the existing machinery. Only the few ticks near the threshold matter (about 2 to 3 on loopmm), not all.

The mechanism to resolve which case holds is small enough that it likely does **not** need full B&B: a simple **active-set fixed point** (assume a zeroing pattern, solve, recompute which ticks actually fell below threshold, repeat to self-consistency) is the cheap default. A disjunctive branch is the fallback if the fixed point oscillates. This sub-task is independently shippable and improves seed fidelity regardless of which basin method wins below.

## Sub-task 2: strengthen the recovery so it reaches the right basin (the open question)

This is where the recovery is genuinely degenerate (loopmm's 0.245 continuous violation) and where the method is **not yet decided**. Candidates:

- **Bound-pruned branch and bound** (leading candidate). Branch on the undetermined seam variables (pin a band on an intermediate cross height, re-solve the tail), convex dual per node, `dualBound` to prune, `SlpSolve` as the per-leaf in-basin closer. The case for it: (1) the only method that empirically works on loopmm, `EarlyCrossSweep`, is already a 1-variable unpruned form of this, so it is the generalization of the proven success; (2) the convex bound is tight here (3e-5), which is the precondition that makes pruning effective; (3) local methods are measured to fail (SLP stays in-basin, ILS/CMA plateau at the basin wall); (4) it yields the optimality certificate (the gap). Risks: NP-hard worst case, may not converge in budget on long sections; branching-variable selection is itself a heuristic.
- **Structured global search** (basin-hopping / diversity-injected ILS). Simpler, bundleable, no certificate. Plain ILS failed; structured diversity (which is what `EarlyCrossSweep` injects) worked. Essentially B&B without the bound pruning.
- **Extend `EarlyCrossSweep`** to sweep more than one seam variable, no pruning. Simplest; may suffice for a few cycles; degrades as the variable product grows (the case pruning is meant to fix).
- **Graph of Convex Sets (GCS).** Better-suited when basins are spatial homotopy (the j154 / desert-hard family), a worse fit for loopmm's velocity-sacrifice basins. Worth keeping in mind for the obstacle family, not the primary candidate here.

## Deliverables (in order)

1. **Inertia folding (sub-task 1)** plus a test that the inertia term drops out of the recovered path on loopmm. Independently mergeable.
2. **A miss-screen and fixture set.** Use the dual-bound gap (`dualBound` minus best feasible found) across the capture library, plus the claimed multi-cycle loop-mm case, to assemble a set of reachable-but-currently-missed jumps. One fixture (loopmm) is too thin to choose a method.
3. **A bake-off** of the sub-task 2 candidates (extend-EarlyCrossSweep vs bound-pruned B&B vs structured global) on that set, scored on does-it-reach-the-bound and cost. Pick the winner from data, then build it. Do not commit to B&B before this.

## Reuse

- `ClosedFormSolve` (recover + margin ladder), `CostateDualSolver` (costates / dual value), `JumpLinearModel` (`compileWalls`, `coef`, `constPos`, `mMagAll`, `objectiveVectors`), `SlpSolve` (in-basin primal closer), `ExactJumpModel` (per-axis inertia via `forMcVersion`, plus the inertia-off variant `new ExactJumpModel(0.0, perAxis, modern)` used to isolate the term), `EarlyCrossSweep` (#186, the 1-variable precursor of branch type used in sub-task 2).
- Diagnostics from this investigation: `DualBoundCoverageTest` (per-capture `dualBound` NaN scan) and `DualBoundTrajectoryTest` (recovery trajectory, continuous-space feasibility, sine/inertia decomposition).

## Out of scope

- Dedicated byte-exact lattice repair (sphere-decode / CVP). The measurement demotes it: after inertia folds in, the residual is approximately 1e-5, which the existing margin ladder handles. Revisit only if a measured residual-landing problem remains.
- Backward reachability (#178).
- Relationship to #186: its `EarlyCrossSweep` is the current 1-D precursor for sub-task 2; this issue is the general recovery. They merge once the method is chosen.

## Test plan

- `:core:test`, headless. Add a `solve` or `closedform` sidecar asserting the recovery is continuous-feasible and near-bound on the degenerate case.
- Re-run the mismatch decomposition on loopmm and confirm the inertia term is removed.
- No loader `runClient` needed; core solver work, gated by the byte-exact model.
title: feat: stronger step-1 path recovery after the dual bound (inertia-aware, near-bound)
